name: Silk amino acids

lead: Silk amino acids are the small peptides and free amino acids obtained by breaking down silk protein. Silk fibroin is built from a repeating glycine-serine-glycine-alanine pattern, with glycine about half of it [1].

The appearance angle is indirect. In sport nutrition research, a trial in elite fin-swimmers reported lower lactate responses and improved stamina measures, which could support training volume; the protein is also used in cosmetic products for a smoother feel [2][3].

paras: It is taken as a powder or drink supplement in the studies, and applied as an ingredient in shampoos, conditioners and skin products. In the swimmer trial it was mixed with a carbohydrate drink before training sessions [2].
The published trials describe it as well tolerated; the Sil-Q1 study called it a safe functional food supplement [3]. Data are limited to small study populations.

chain: Amino acid hydrolysate taken around training
Lower lactate build-up reported in swimmers
angle.text: Studied as a stamina aid for athletes and as an immune supplement; any physique benefit would come through training capacity.

lead: Silk amino acids, also called silk peptide or silk amino acid hydrolysate, are produced by hydrolysing silk protein. Silk fibroin is built from a repeating Gly-Ser-Gly-Ala-Gly-Ala sequence with about 50% glycine, and sericin is the glue-like coating [1].

A 2014 randomised trial in elite male fin-swimmers found that supplementation with silk amino acids was associated with changes in lactate and a small gain in swimming velocity at a fixed lactate level compared with the carbohydrate drink alone [2]. A 2021 trial of 130 Korean adults found that a silk peptide (Sil-Q1) raised natural killer cell activity versus placebo over eight weeks [3].

For appearance, the route is indirect: better stamina or recovery could support training, and silk proteins are also used as ingredients in hair and skin cosmetics. The studies themselves measured performance and immune markers, not physique or skin.

paras: Fibroin's repeating Gly-Ser-Gly-Ala-Gly-Ala sequence forms beta-pleated sheets, and glycine makes up about half, allowing tight packing; alanine and serine add strength [1]. Sericin, the sticky coating, is 20 to 30% of the fibre by weight depending on the source [1].
Supplement studies cover stamina in swimmers and immune activity [2][3]. Research on silk peptides also covers wound-healing microspheres and a gerbil cognition model [4][5].

In a randomised trial of elite fin-swimmers, silk amino acids at 500 mg/kg body mass, taken three times daily before training in a carbohydrate drink, lowered lactate response and shifted the lactate-velocity curve [2]. In 130 adults, 7.5 g of Sil-Q1 for eight weeks increased NK cell cytotoxicity and IL-12 compared with placebo [3].
